item.title: Tax junk food, kava and alcohol instead of hospital fees
item.description: Health sector leaders and former policymakers have rejected ideas for introducing hospital user fees in Fiji, saying many families are already struggling with the rising cost of living and would face further hardship if required to pay for healthcare services. item.content:encoded:
Health sector leaders and former policymakers have rejected ideas for introducing hospital user fees in Fiji, saying many families are already struggling with the rising cost of living and would face further hardship if required to pay for healthcare services. When questioned whether people should start paying for health services in hospitals as one of the ways for funding healthcare especially those living in urban settings, President of the Fiji College of General Practitioners, Dr Dhirend Lal, says charging people for hospital services is not recommended at a time when the country is already facing a hardships. Lal says instead the government should consider introducing a five percent tax on products such as junk food, kava, sugar drinks and alcohol to generate additional revenue for the health sector. Following Lal's suggetions former Minister for Health and Medical Services Dr Ifereimi Waqainabete also believes that introducing healthcare charges could place significant pressure on vulnerable families. Dr Waqainabete says there are people living in poverty along the Suva-Nausori corridor, and requiring them to pay for healthcare could push some households further into crisis. He says targeted taxation on certain products could be a better alternative for raising funds for the healthcare system. Meanwhile, Fiji Medical Association President Dr Ronal Kumar says healthcare is not cheap, therefore rather than introducing charges for patients, greater emphasis should be placed on encouraging people to take responsibility for their health and prevent illnesses.

Former Attorney-General and Minister for Economy Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum says a system requiring some people to contribute towards their healthcare costs could be considered in the future. However, he says it should not be introduced immediately or applied to all Fijians, given the current economic challenges and financial pressures facing households. Sayed-Khaiyum says higher-income earners could potentially be required to pay for their own treatment, or have the costs covered by their private health insurance, instead of relying entirely on Government funding.

item.title: At least 30 missing after inter-island ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 13/09/2026 Vanuatu authorities have been searching for survivors after an inter-island ferry carrying 34 passengers and 11 crew members sank in rough weather on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 13/09/2026

Vanuatu authorities have been searching for survivors after an inter-island ferry carrying 34 passengers and 11 crew members sank in rough weather on Friday.

ABC Pacific reports that seven people have been rescued, with an estimated 38 still unaccounted for , as boats and a Flying Doctor plane search for more survivors, 24 hours after the vessel sank in the north of the country.

Police told national broadcaster VBCTC that the MV Matui sank in rough seas on Friday while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo.

Police said one survivor made it to shore on the island of Santo, where a diver took him to the local community for help.

A video showing the man, named Jefferson, covered in a blanket and being offered a cup of hot tea, has been widely shared on social media.

There have also been calls for communities along the coast of Ambae to keep an eye out for possible survivors and assist as the search continues.

Former Foreign Minister Matai Seremaiah, who was aboard the vessel LC Mahalia, rescued a number of survivors.

He posted on Facebook that two additional survivors had been spotted by a plane, although darkness made their retrieval difficult.

Flying Doctor Mark Turnbull used his plane to drop life jackets and helped locate survivors for rescue vessels.

Terry Ngwele, harbour master of Luganville on the island of Santo, who was aboard another rescue vessel, said the search would continue tomorrow.

He told ABC News that they rescued two people today.
